newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Court allows reimbursement of illegal dock dues.
newsitem.headline: Court allows reimbursement of illegal dock dues.

text.p: The European Court of Justice said on Tuesday traders who paid illegal customs fees in the form of dock dues may recover those payments from member states, unless such recovery would amount to unjust enrichment.

Dock dues are generally passed on by traders to their customers, as part of the purchase price of goods. The court said today those fees, determined by prior decisions to be illegal customs duties under Community rules, are recoverable by traders unless the member state can show the fees were paid by customers.
National courts will have to decide the facts in each case, the court said, to determine who paid the fees, and if a reimbursement would unjustly enrich the trader.
Traders might also bring damage claims under national law, where such remedies exist, to prove the illegal duties increased the price of goods and resulted in the loss of sales.
The court mentioned individuals' rights to bring damage claims in national courts, under the Factortame and Brasserie du Pecheur decisions, for member state breaches of Community law.
(Court translation into English. Original language of the case: French)
"Dock dues - Recovery of sums not due - Obligation to pass on the charge - Overseas departments"
Reference from the Tribunal d'Instance, Paris for a ruling between

Societes: Comateb, Panigua, Edouard et Fils, Distribution de Vins et Liequers, Etablissements Andre Haan, Diffusion Generale de Quincaillerie, Diffusion Generale, Cama Renault, SCP Ovide et Dorville, Societe Ducros Guadeloupe, Societe Comptoir Commercial Caraible, Giafa, LVS, Catherine et Jean-Claude Tabar Nouval, l'Heure et l'Or, General Bazar Bricolage, Granin d'Or, Cash Service, Etablissements Efira, Farandole, Carat, Rio, Guadaloupeenne de Distribuion Moderne, Martinique Automobiles, Socovi, Etablissements Gabriel Vangour et Cie SARL, Simat Guadeloupe SARL
Directeur General des Douanes et Droits Indirect
on the interpretation of Community law concerning repayment of sums not due

1. A member state may resist repayment to the trader of a charge levied in breach of Community law only where it is established that the charge has been borne in its entirety by another person and that reimbursement of the trader would constitute unjust enrichment. It is for the national courts to determine, in the light of the facts in each case, whether those conditions have been satisfied. If the burden of the charge has been passed on only in part, it is for the national authorities to reimburse the trader the amount not passed on.

2. The fact that there is a legal obligation to incorporate the charge in the cost price does not mean that there is a presumption that the entire charge has been passed on, even where failure to comply with that obligation carries a penalty.

3. Where, although the charge has been passed on to the purchaser, domestic law permits the trader to claim that the illegal levying of the charge has caused him damage which excludes, in whole or in part, any unjust enrichment, it is for the national court to give such effect to the claim as may be appropriate.
